title: Design Parking System
description: Brute force to optimized: tracking individual parked cars in lists versus three simple integer counters.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a parking system for a parking lot with three sizes of spots: big, medium, and small, each with a fixed number of slots. Implement addCar(carType), which returns true and parks the car if a slot of the matching type is available, or false if not, given carType 1 for big, 2 for medium, 3 for small.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","Constructor: big, medium, small slot counts. Then a sequence of addCar(carType) calls"],["Output","true if the car is parked, false if that type is full"],["Goal","Track available slots per car type with O(1) operations"],["Constraints","0 <= big, medium, small <= 1000, at most 1000 calls to addCar"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Three independent, fixed-capacity categories being tracked","A simple counter per category, decremented on use"],["\"Is there room, and if so, take it\" repeated queries","O(1) check-and-decrement, no need for any complex structure"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Each car type has its own independent slot pool. Parking a car of a given type only affects that type's remaining slot count, and the only thing that matters is whether at least one slot of the matching type remains, not which specific slot it is.

blocks.title: Analogy: Three Separate Ticket Counters with Limited Seats
blocks.text: Picture three separate ticket counters (one each for big, medium, and small vehicles), each starting with a fixed number of seats. Selling a ticket at one counter has no effect on the other two, and the counter simply refuses once its own seats run out.

blocks.caption: Three independent counters, one per car type, is all that is needed

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: big=1, medium=1, small=0, addCar calls = [1, 2, 3, 1]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Result","Explanation"],"rows":[["addCar(1)","true","Big slot available, parked, 0 big slots remain"],["addCar(2)","true","Medium slot available, parked, 0 medium slots remain"],["addCar(3)","false","No small slots exist (small=0), rejected"],["addCar(1)","false","No big slots remain, rejected"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before considering any list or set to track individual parked cars, notice the ONLY thing that ever matters is how many slots of each type remain, which is fully captured by three simple integer counters.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The specific identity of a parked car is never asked about, only whether a slot of a given type is available right now.

Observation 2: This means the exact count of remaining slots per type is a complete and sufficient representation of the system's state.

Observation 3: addCar(carType) becomes simply: check if the counter for that type is greater than zero; if so, decrement it and return true; otherwise return false.

Observation 4: No slot needs to ever be "freed" in this version of the problem (no removeCar operation), so the counters only ever decrease.
This leads to maintaining three simple integer counters, one per car type, checked and decremented directly in O(1) per addCar call.
6. Brute Force Solution
Maintain a list of parked cars for each type, and check the list's length against the type's capacity before adding a new entry.
Step by step algorithm

items: Maintain three lists, one per car type, each recording every car parked there.
On addCar(carType), check whether the corresponding list's length is less than its capacity.
If there is room, append a new entry to that list and return true; otherwise return false.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Tracking individual parked cars in a list directly mirrors a literal mental model of "cars in a lot."
This uses O(total cars parked) space and O(1) amortized time per call, but the list itself is unnecessary since car identities are never queried.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) per addCar call (list append and length check).
Space: O(total cars parked over the system's lifetime).
Limitation: storing individual car entries wastes memory, since only the COUNT of remaining slots per type is ever needed; three simple counters achieve the same correctness in O(1) space per type.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why storing individual entries is unnecessary: addCar never needs to know WHICH cars are parked, only whether room remains for a given type.

The direct simplification: replace each type's list with a single integer counter, initialized to that type's capacity, and decrement it whenever a car of that type is successfully parked.

The check-and-decrement logic: addCar(carType) simply checks if the counter is greater than zero; if so, decrement and return true, otherwise return false.

The core idea: three plain integer counters fully capture everything the problem ever asks about.
Maintain three integers (one per car type), each initialized to that type's slot count. addCar checks if the matching counter is positive; if so, decrement it and return true, otherwise return false.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for big=1, medium=1, small=0

blocks.caption: Three plain integer counters, checked and decremented in O(1) per call

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since the only question ever asked is "is a slot of this type available," and the only action ever taken is "occupy one such slot," a plain integer count per type fully and correctly captures the system's entire state, with no need to track individual car identities at all.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) per addCar call.
Space: O(1), just three integers.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Design Parking System is a clean example of recognizing that a problem only cares about AGGREGATE counts, not individual entity identities, letting a much simpler counter-based design replace a naive list-based one.
Common Mistakes

items: Using a 0-indexed array without accounting for carType values starting at 1, causing an off-by-one indexing error.
Overcomplicating the design with unnecessary tracking structures when simple counters fully suffice.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A car type initialized with 0 slots","Every addCar call for that type immediately returns false."],["Many consecutive addCar calls for the same type","Each succeeds until the counter reaches zero, then all subsequent calls for that type fail."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Recognizing quickly that "only counts matter here, not identities" and proposing the minimal counter-based design upfront demonstrates good judgment about appropriate solution complexity.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "track availability across a few fixed categories", think: simple integer counters, one per category, checked and decremented in O(1).
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you add a removeCar operation to free up a slot?
How would this design change if there were many more categories, or categories added dynamically?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "track remaining capacity across a small, fixed set of categories" design problem.
Design HashSet and similar minimal-state design problems that reward recognizing the simplest sufficient representation.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches run in O(1) time per call; the counter-based approach uses O(1) space versus O(total cars parked) for the list-based approach, making it strictly better here.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: represent state with the minimal sufficient aggregate (counters), not individual entity tracking.
Core Idea: maintain one integer counter per car type; addCar checks and decrements it directly in O(1).
Time: O(1) per call for both approaches.
Space: O(total cars parked) for the list-based approach, O(1) for the counter-based approach.
Most Important Observation: since car identities are never queried, only counts matter, making simple counters the correct minimal design.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible, beginner-friendly design problem about choosing the right level of abstraction.
One line memory trick: three counters, check and decrement.
